outcomes: Separates an observation (what you can point to) from a guess (a prediction or judgment)
Knows that some guesses can be tested
Writes down one unsure moment per game
sources: docs/council-synthesis.md CD-11, CD-12 (observe before judging; Botvinnik, Dvoretsky, Rowson recalled [R]); Guardian study ch. 18, 23 (user's document: noticing uncertainty; observation versus explanation)

docs/citable-views.md 10.4 and 10.5 (Dan Heisman, Hope Chess, paraphrased [S]); 10.10 (Capablanca on his own thinking failures, paraphrased [V-sheet CI-51]); 10.13 (Silman: an engine shows what to play but not why, paraphrased [S]); 10.9 (E. Lasker, count attackers and defenders with values [V-sheet K2])

positions: Lichess 2013-01 game ha48pwvj (CC0) for the two middlegame boards; the opening trap board is authored by replaying legal moves with python-chess; engine claims at the validator's recorded depth
[H] and [I] marks in the text are conjecture by the author, not results

steps.caption: A position from a Lichess game [R, not rechecked], White to move. Before any opinion, just look. The black knight on d4 is marked.
The knight attacks eight squares. Two of them hold White pieces: the queen on f3 and the pawn on c2. A careful count gives the same answer every time.

steps.text: **Look first.** What you just did is an **observation**: something you can point to on the board, so a careful count gives anyone the same answer. A **guess** is a prediction or a judgment, such as 'I am winning' or 'he will take my pawn'. Guesses are fine. The skill is knowing which of the two you are writing down.

**Why bother separating them?** A misread board and a misjudged future need different fixes: recount the first, test the second. Even a count can slip, such as calling a pawn twice defended when it is defended three times, so recount. Untested guesses become mistakes, as the f7 trap will show. [H] Labelling a guess may slow you enough to look for the reply you hoped would not come.

steps.caption: Observation one. The knight attacks the queen on f3. One White pawn, on g2, defends that square. You can count both on the board.

Observation two. The knight also attacks the pawn on c2, and no White piece defends it. A piece that is attacked and has no defender is **loose**. (Books often use 'loose' for any undefended piece; here we use the narrower sense.)

Observation three. The pawn on e4 is attacked once, by the knight on f6, and defended three times. That is the count. Whether the pawn is safe is a guess; you would test it. [I] The count changes if a defender, such as the queen, is taken.

steps.text: Now the other kind. 'I am lost' feels like a fact because the feeling is strong, but it is a judgment about the future. So is 'my queen is safe, because a pawn defends it'. Write guesses down too, but **label them as guesses**. Next you will see how a guess can be tested, with a worked example first.

steps.caption: Three notes about this position. One: the knight attacks my queen. Two: my queen is safe, a pawn defends it. Three: I am lost. Only the first can be read straight off the board. Notes two and three are guesses.
A worked test of note two, 'my queen is safe'. Play it out: let White ignore the knight with a quiet move, and see what happens.

line.say: White ignores the knight and plays a quiet pawn move.
The knight takes the queen and attacks the king.
The pawn takes the knight. White gave a queen for a knight, so the guess failed.

steps.text: **Three ways to test a guess.** Count the attackers and defenders. Play the line out and add up what each side takes. Or ask an **engine**, a chess program that calculates far deeper than you can. One warning from the last board: a defended piece is not always safe, because a cheaper attacker can still win a dearer piece.

steps.caption: Another guess: 'I can move the queen anywhere, it will be fine.' Test one square, g3.

line.say: The queen steps away, but c2 stays loose.
The knight takes the pawn with check and also attacks the rook on a1.
The king steps aside.
The knight takes the rook. White has lost a pawn and a rook so far; the engine rates it about -3 pawns for White at depth 18.

steps.caption: The test of that guess. The bishop takes the pawn with check, and the king takes the bishop.

line.say: The bishop takes a pawn and gives check.
The king takes the bishop. White gave 3 for 1.

steps.caption: Now test the guess 'the queen to d1 is my best move'. The engine agrees, and the move does two jobs.

line.say: The queen leaves the knight's reach and guards the pawn on c2, so no White piece is attacked and unguarded any more.
Black makes a quiet move.
White castles: the king is safe and the rook joins in.

steps.caption: The guess 'I am lost' tested: the engine rates this position as close to level. [H] A queen under attack is vivid, and a vivid danger may make the whole position feel worse than it is. That is a hypothesis, not a result.

steps.title: Guesses can be tested
steps.prompt: Compare a confirmed guess, a refuted guess and an observation. For a guess, predict whether a test will confirm it, then check.

steps.caption: A quiet moment in the same game, one move earlier. 'I can castle now' is an observation, because the board allows it. 'Castling feels scary' is a feeling. It is real, but it is about you, not about this board.

steps.text: **Three boxes.** Some notes are observations, settled by looking. Some are guesses you can test. Some are feelings the board cannot answer, such as 'I feel nervous'. [I] A feeling is still worth one line in your notes, because it shows where you were unsure. Just do not write it in the observation box.

steps.caption: Testing the note 'Black will win my e4 pawn'. White actually played d3 here, adding a third guard. Black takes the pawn anyway.

line.say: White adds a third guard to the pawn on e4.
Black takes the pawn with the knight.
The pawn takes the knight, which nothing defends. Black gave a knight for a pawn, so this try fails.

steps.caption: A beginner trap. White's queen and bishop both look at the pawn on f7. Black to move.
Suppose Black replies with a knight move that attacks the queen, thinking 'she must run' [I] a typical beginner thought. That is a guess, and nobody tested it. Now White moves.

line.say: The queen takes f7. The bishop guards her, so the king cannot take her and has nowhere to go: checkmate.

steps.text: Dan Heisman called this **Hope Chess** [S: Heisman, chess.com article on Hope Chess]: you make a move and hope the opponent has no strong reply, without first checking their forcing replies: checks, captures and threats. Black's note was a guess, 'she must run', and it was never tested. Before you move, name your guess, then look at every forcing reply the other side has.

steps.caption: What testing would have found. The pawn move attacks the queen first, so Black keeps control.

line.say: The pawn attacks the queen and gives her a reason to move.
The queen steps back and still eyes f7.
The knight develops and blocks the f-file, so only the bishop still looks at f7.

steps.caption: More than one answer works. The queen to e7 adds a second defender, so f7 is now attacked twice and defended twice.

line.say: The queen becomes a second defender of f7, next to the king.

steps.caption: A model note. Move 9. I could see: the knight attacks my queen, one pawn defends the queen, the pawn on c2 is loose. I guessed: the queen is safe, because it is defended. What would settle it: let the knight take the queen and count what each side loses.

Another model note, from the black side. Move 3. I could see: two white pieces attack f7, one black piece defends it. I guessed: if I attack the queen she must run. What would settle it: list White's checks and captures after my move.

steps.text: **One unsure moment per game.** After a game, pick one move where you felt unsure and write four lines: the move number, what you could see, what you guessed, and what would settle it. Skip the engine for now. One short note beats a long review you never finish. [H] Keeping to one moment may make the habit easier to keep. It is a habit to try.

steps.caption: Where the first model note came from, so you can find its move number. White's eighth move adds a guard of e4. Black's reply puts the knight on d4, and the next move is the unsure moment: move 9.

line.say: White's eighth move: another guard for the pawn on e4.
Black's eighth move: the knight jumps to d4, attacking the queen and the pawn on c2.

steps.text: **Be honest in the note.** Capablanca (Chess Fundamentals, Part II) openly names ways his own thinking failed, such as judging a combination unsound and then losing to it. Silman, as reported on chess.com [S] and not checked in his own books, says an engine shows what to play but not why: test a guess with it, then explain the result yourself. Both are paraphrases.

steps.caption: Check yourself. No hints.

steps.text: **Say it back.** An observation is something I can point to on the board, like who attacks what and who defends it. A guess is a prediction or a judgment, like 'I am lost'; I label it and test it if I can. After a game I write down one unsure moment: what I saw, what I guessed, and what would settle it.

steps.prompt: Use your last game, or any position from this lesson. Pick ONE moment where you were unsure and fill in the four lines. Keep observation and guess apart.
